Intercropping cereals with fodder legume crops like cowpea
and ricebean is a practice in the semi-arid tropics of India to
reduce the fragility and uncertainty of agricultural production
systems under rainfed upland situations. These systems
produce a considerable amount of biomass that can be
incorporated into the soil, transferring nutrients from the
crops to soil and enriching the organic carbon content. --Maize and other forage legumes such as sesbania,
cowpea, pigeonpea, ricebean, and mungbean are important
short-duration crops which provide more economic return
to growers than long-duration crops

lentil was relay intercropped into the
already developed durum wheat (at the tillering stage), thus minimizing early competition
with the main crop while maximizing resource facilitation and sharing at the later stages of
both intercrops. This study showed that despite contrasting climatic conditions, intercropping of winter
durum wheat with spring lentil can increase the overall aboveground biomass and grain
production per unit area compared to sole crops. No adverse competition effects between
the intercrops were observed, hence a yield advantage in both intercropping systems over
the sole crops. The complementary functional traits of durum wheat–lentil
intercrops effectively controlled weeds comparable to mechanical hoeing.
